sources.title: Siege of Toulon
Evacuation of Toulon, 1793 (showing many ships on fire)
View of Toulon, 1793
Les blessures de Napoléon (Xavier Riaud)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 1793 military defeats and the fall of the Girondins brought the Montagnards to power, and federalist and royalist revolts broke out in the provinces. In Toulon, the main French naval base and arsenal on the Mediterranean, royalists negotiated with the British admiral Lord Hood.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: On 27–28 August 1793 Toulon was handed to an Anglo-Spanish fleet under Hood and Lángara in the name of the child Louis XVII, together with a large part of the French Mediterranean fleet. The base's strategic value and the Revolution's prestige both demanded its recapture.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The republicans needed to retake the port and its ships; the allies needed to keep the anchorage safe. Britannica credits Bonaparte with the plan that Dugommier carried out: to take the forts commanding the anchorage, so that the fleet could not stay, rather than storm the city.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Toulon's harbour is ringed by heights and forts. Whoever held the forts commanding the anchorage could fire on the ships inside it.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: General Carteaux began the siege; General Dugommier directed it from November. Bonaparte took over the artillery when its commander was wounded, a post he owed to the commissioner Saliceti. The allied garrison included British, Spanish and Neapolitan troops, commanded from November by General O'Hara.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Through the autumn the republicans built up batteries on the heights around the city, while the allies held the forts and kept their fleet in the harbour.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The siege began in early September and was pressed slowly until Dugommier arrived. On 30 November an allied sortie against French batteries was thrown back and O'Hara was captured. On the night of 16–17 December, under heavy bombardment, the republicans stormed the forts commanding the anchorage, including Fort Mulgrave, where Bonaparte was wounded in the thigh. On 18 December French guns opened fire on the fleet, and the allies evacuated.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Dugommier's adoption of Bonaparte's plan to strike at the forts above the anchorage, rather than the city's defences, was decisive. Hood's decision to evacuate, taking refugees with him and ordering the arsenal and ships burned, followed once the anchorage was under fire.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of the forts over the anchorage made the harbour untenable for the allied fleet.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The allies embarked their troops and many thousands of inhabitants who feared the republicans' vengeance. Ships and much of the arsenal were set on fire, but the destruction was only partly achieved, and a sizable part of the fleet was later recovered and repaired.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Republican troops entered on 19 December, and the reprisals were severe: Jacobins coming out to welcome them were cut down, royalists were rounded up and shot or bayoneted, and special tribunals under representatives of the Convention, among them Barras, Fréron and Augustin Robespierre, sent many more to their deaths. The Convention proposed renaming the city and razing its civilian buildings. On 22 December Bonaparte was promoted to brigadier general. Among the ships that survived was L'Orient, later destroyed at the Nile.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Attacking what makes an enemy's position untenable can achieve more than attacking the position itself: a naval base is held from the heights around it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Later legend magnified Bonaparte's part. Britannica credits him with the plan; the Royal Museums Greenwich catalogue says only that he played a notable role. The date of his wound is given as 16 or 17 December, and the extent of the fleet's destruction is reported differently. The scale of the reprisals is not quantified here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's article, read in a browser, gives the fullest narrative. The Royal Museums Greenwich and Royal Collection catalogue entries describe an eyewitness drawing and a contemporary print of the evacuation, and Xavier Riaud's article for the Fondation Napoléon covers Bonaparte's wound. Campaign histories such as Chandler's were not read.

sources.title: De Paris à Milan, mars–mai 1796 (Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien 406)
La 1ère campagne d'Italie : chronologie
Il y a 230 ans, les premières victoires de la campagne d'Italie (Pierre Branda)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Army of Italy, formed in 1792, had spent 1793–1795 fighting at heavy cost in the Alpine passes. On 2 March 1796 the Directory gave Bonaparte its command, and he took over at Nice on 27 March.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The army was strung out along the coast. Facing it, Colli's Sardinian army lay around Ceva and Mondovì and Beaulieu's Austrians further east, each with its own line of retreat. The allies themselves planned an offensive into Provence with British naval support.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Bonaparte planned to cross the Apennines by the Cadibona pass, seize the ground between the two allied armies and defeat each in turn. The Fondation Napoléon article says he had proposed such a plan in 1794, and credits Carnot with the principle of concentrating force on a main theatre.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The campaign was fought in the Ligurian Apennines and the upper valleys of the Bormida and Tanaro, among ridges, castles and narrow valleys. Branda notes that the Austrian corps at Montenotte held high ground but was poorly linked to its rear and far from the Piedmontese.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The article says Bonaparte's mobile forces had fewer infantry than the allies, little cavalry and far fewer guns. His divisions were led by Masséna, Laharpe, Augereau and Sérurier. The allies were dispersed in winter quarters, with detachments under d'Argenteau and Provera linking Beaulieu's Austrians to Colli's Sardinians. The strengths the article gives are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Bonaparte feinted toward Turin and Alessandria and left a brigade at Voltri as a deception. Beaulieu attacked Voltri on 10 April, and d'Argenteau moved against Monte Legino, which a small French force held.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 12 April Laharpe attacked d'Argenteau frontally at Montenotte while Masséna came on his flank, and the Austrians retreated. Augereau took Millesimo on 13 April, and the Piedmontese in the castle of Cosseria surrendered. Masséna took Dego, lost it to an Austrian counterattack on 15 April and recovered it. Bonaparte then turned on the Piedmontese: after checks at Ceva and on the flooded Tanaro, Colli was driven from Mondovì.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte chose to defeat the Sardinians first, against the Directory's instruction to strike the Austrians, arguing that Colli was closest and threatened his communications. He shifted his supply line to cover the advance.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The separation of the two allied armies after Montenotte, Millesimo and Dego left Colli to face the concentrated French army alone.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: By the armistice of Cherasco on 28 April 1796, the King of Sardinia left the coalition, handed over Coni, Tortona and Alessandria with their artillery and stores, and granted passage over the Po.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Peace with Piedmont-Sardinia followed in May, ceding Savoy and Nice to France. The army's supply line was shortened, and Bonaparte could turn on Beaulieu in Lombardy. Branda notes that Bonaparte's letters to the Directory, reprinted in French newspapers, began to build his public image; he later said his nobility dated from Montenotte.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Striking the hinge between two allied armies whose interests and lines of retreat diverged let a weaker army defeat each in turn: the strategy of the central position.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: How far the plan was Bonaparte's own is debated; the article traces it to his earlier proposals while acknowledging Carnot's principles. The article also shows how the official version was shaped: credit for holding Monte Legino went to Rampon, and the famous proclamation to the army at Nice was probably reconstructed later. The date of Mondovì is given as 21 or 22 April. Bonaparte's claims of prisoners and captured guns are not repeated.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main narrative is the Fondation Napoléon's article from the Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien, which draws on Corda, Colin and others and criticizes Napoleon's later Saint Helena accounts as unreliable. Its chronology and Pierre Branda's 2026 chronicle add dates and the role of publicity.

sources.title: De Paris à Milan, mars–mai 1796 (Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien 406)
Lodi
La 1ère campagne d'Italie : chronologie

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Cherasco Bonaparte turned against Beaulieu's Austrian army. Instead of forcing the Po at Valenza, he made a surprise crossing near Piacenza while Sérurier made visible preparations at Valenza.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bonaparte concluded an armistice with the Duke of Parma for money and food. On the night of 9–10 May General Laharpe was killed at Codogno in confused fighting, the article says almost certainly by French fire.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Bonaparte aimed to cut off Beaulieu's retreat west of the Adda. Beaulieu had already crossed, leaving a rearguard under Sebottendorf to hold the bridge at Lodi.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Lodi is a small Lombard city south-east of Milan on the Adda. The single bridge was the focus of the fighting; the present bridge stands a little south of the 1796 one.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Sebottendorf's rearguard held the far bank with infantry and guns. Bonaparte's advance guard included elite battalions and cavalry, and Masséna's troops reached the bridge. The strengths given in the article are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Bonaparte sent cavalry to ford the river upstream and placed guns to cover the bridge so that it could not be destroyed.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 10 May a grenadier column, led by its generals, crossed the bridge under heavy fire, while cavalry under Beaumont and Ordener crossed above the city and struck the Austrian flank. The rearguard withdrew, leaving prisoners and guns.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte combined a frontal assault across the bridge with a cavalry crossing upstream, accepting the risk of an attack under fire rather than waiting for the flanking move alone.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The grenadiers' crossing, together with the cavalry on the flank, broke the rearguard.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The bridge was taken, but Beaulieu's main army had already escaped; the Fondation Napoléon article calls the success incomplete because Bonaparte arrived too late.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory opened the road to Milan, which Bonaparte entered in mid-May. He wrote to Carnot on 11 May that the battle had given the Republic all of Italy, and Lodi earned him the nickname of the Little Corporal.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A tactically daring action can matter more for morale and reputation than for its operational result: Lodi took a bridge but missed the army it was meant to trap.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Accounts of who led the storming column differ; the article says only that the generals led it, and the places page credits Masséna with getting across. Napoleon's later claim that Lodi revealed his destiny is not documented in the sources read here. The entry into Milan is dated 15 or 16 May.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon's article from the Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien gives the narrative, its places page describes the site and quotes Bonaparte's letter to Carnot, and its chronology supplies dates.

sources.title: De Mantoue à Tolentino, juin 1796 – février 1797 (Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien 410)
La 1ère campagne d'Italie : chronologie
Wurmser, Dagobert Sigismond, comte de (Daniel Reichel, Dictionnaire Napoléon)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Lodi the French blockaded Mantua; the chronology dates the start of the siege to 18 July 1796. Wurmser, a veteran Austrian marshal, replaced Beaulieu and was reinforced from the Rhine to relieve the fortress.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Holding the siege tied much of Bonaparte's army to cordon posts around Mantua, and Wurmser's biography says he believed it would keep Bonaparte pinned.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Wurmser divided his army: Quasdanovich came down the Chiese valley west of Lake Garda while Wurmser came down the Adige to the east, both converging on Mantua. Bonaparte's aim was to concentrate against each column before they could unite.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Lake Garda separated the two Austrian columns, which could not support each other. The main battle was fought between Solferino and Castiglione, south of the lake, with Wurmser's right on the Solferino heights and his left on the plain.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Bonaparte had divisions under Masséna, Augereau, Sérurier, Sauret and Despinoy and a reserve under Kilmaine that included Marmont's horse artillery. Wurmser and Quasdanovich led the two Austrian columns. The article's strengths are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Wurmser faced west across the Brescia–Mantua road. Bonaparte planned a frontal attack by Augereau and Masséna, a flank attack by Sérurier's division brought up from Marcaria by way of Guidizzolo, and a decisive thrust by Kilmaine's reserve.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 29–30 July the Austrian columns drove in the French covering posts, took Brescia and threatened Bonaparte's communications. He lifted the siege of Mantua on 30 July, abandoning siege equipment, and turned on Quasdanovich, whose columns were beaten around Lonato, Salò and Brescia; the fighting of 3 August kept the Austrian columns apart. On 5 August Bonaparte attacked Wurmser at Castiglione.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte's decision to give up the siege and sacrifice its equipment in order to concentrate his army was decisive and remains controversial.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Sérurier's flank attack shook the Austrians, and Kilmaine's reserve then made the decisive attack.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Wurmser retreated across the Mincio and the Adige toward Trent. The French, exhausted by days of forced marching, could not pursue, and the siege of Mantua was resumed on 7 August.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Wurmser tried again in September, was defeated at Bassano and ended up shut inside Mantua, which surrendered early in 1797; Bonaparte granted him the honours of war.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Interior lines let a commander strike separated enemy forces one after another, but only by giving up secondary objectives; here the siege train was the price.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Gouvion Saint-Cyr, quoted in the Fondation Napoléon article, argued that the siege train could have been withdrawn in time and that its loss tied the army to Mantua for months; the article itself judges the decision consistent with Bonaparte's principles. Napoleon blamed Wurmser for dividing his army. How well the flank attack was timed is not settled by the sources read here. Mantua's surrender is dated 17 January in the chronology and 2 February 1797 elsewhere.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon's article from the Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien gives the narrative and the debate over the siege train; its chronology and Daniel Reichel's biography of Wurmser from the Dictionnaire Napoléon add dates and the Austrian side.

sources.title: De Mantoue à Tolentino, juin 1796 – février 1797 (Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien 410)
Arcole
La 1ère campagne d'Italie : chronologie
Alvinzi, Joseph, baron (Jacques Garnier, Dictionnaire Napoléon)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After two failed Austrian attempts to relieve Mantua, Alvinczi took command in November 1796. The Austrians advanced on two lines: Alvinczi through Friuli and Davidovich down the Adige valley.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Wurmser was shut up in Mantua. Bonaparte had to keep Alvinczi and Davidovich from joining forces.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Unable to break Alvinczi's position at Caldiero frontally, Bonaparte tried to turn it through the marshes by way of Arcole and Villanova, threatening the Austrian rear.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Arcole lies in marshland near the confluence of the Adige and the Alpone, about 20 km south-east of Verona. The fighting was confined to narrow causeways between the marshes and to the bridge over the Alpone.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Bonaparte's forces included Augereau's and Masséna's divisions. Alvinczi commanded the main Austrian army, with Davidovich's force in the Adige valley. The strengths given in the article are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The army left Verona secretly on the evening of 14 November, and Masséna's troops came up by way of Ronco.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 15 November Augereau's attacks on the Arcole bridge failed, and Bonaparte's own attempt to lead his men across did not carry them. Fighting resumed on the 16th and 17th. Bonaparte had a bridge built over the Alpone so that Augereau's divisions could cross and strike the Austrian rear, while Masséna attacked the Arcole bridge again. After three days Alvinczi retreated.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte chose to fight in the marshes, where Austrian numbers could not be deployed, and kept attacking for three days.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The crossing of the Alpone threatened the Austrian rear and, after three days of fighting in which Alvinczi lost many of his best troops, persuaded him to withdraw.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Alvinczi retreated. Joubert defeated Davidovich on 19 November, and Mantua remained isolated.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Alvinczi's next attempt ended at Rivoli in January 1797, and Mantua capitulated soon afterwards. The image of Bonaparte with a flag on the bridge, painted by Gros, became central to his legend, and an obelisk was raised on the site in 1810.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Terrain that restricts movement can cancel numerical superiority, but it also makes attack slow and costly; success came from persistence and a crossing elsewhere.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The flag episode is commemorated on the site and in Gros's painting, but the places page says that on the first day his troops would not follow him; its fame owes much to later propaganda. The story of trumpets sounded behind the Austrian flank does not appear in the sources read here. The chronology dates the decisive day to 17 November.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon's article from the Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien and its places page give the narrative; its chronology and Jacques Garnier's biography of Alvinczi from the Dictionnaire Napoléon add dates and the Austrian commander's career.

Rivoli
French Revolutionary wars: Campaign in Italy
André Masséna, duc de Rivoli, prince d'Essling
Barthélemy-Catherine Joubert

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Austrian attempts to relieve Mantua had failed at Castiglione, Bassano and Arcole. Early in 1797 Alvinczi attacked again, descending the Adige valley, while Provera advanced on Mantua.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Wurmser's army was still shut up in Mantua. A relief army that reached it would threaten Bonaparte's hold on northern Italy; if Mantua fell, the way into Austria lay open.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Alvinczi's main attack aimed to break through at Rivoli while Provera made for Mantua, and two other forces advanced from Friuli on Verona and Legnago. Bonaparte set the secondary threats aside to meet the main attack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Rivoli Veronese stands on the right bank of the Adige, a few miles east of Lake Garda, among steep cliffs with Monte Baldo to the north. The road along the valley floor reached the plateau only by a steep run of hairpin bends, the escalier d'Incanale.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Joubert's division held the plateau, and Bonaparte and Masséna came to its support. Alvinczi attacked in five columns, the fifth carrying all his artillery along the valley road. The Fondation's article credits the French with superiority in artillery; the strengths it gives are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 13 January Joubert, pressed by Alvinczi, fell back on the plateau of Rivoli, and Bonaparte and Masséna marched to his aid.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 14 January the Austrian columns attacked the plateau. Bonaparte concentrated against the fifth column as it climbed from the valley and threw it back in disorder into the ravine. Leaving one of his generals to pursue, he turned with the rest of his forces against Provera and defeated him at La Favorita, at the gates of Mantua, on 16 January. Masséna's division fought three actions between 13 and 16 January and marched for a day and two nights in between.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte left only a screen to check Provera and concentrated everything he could at Rivoli. Once Alvinczi was beaten he regrouped at once against Provera.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The defeat of the column climbing to the plateau, which carried the Austrian artillery, turned Alvinczi's attack into what the Fondation's article calls a bloody disaster.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Alvinczi was routed at Rivoli and Provera capitulated at La Favorita. Wurmser, out of resources, surrendered Mantua.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Papal States were overrun within a fortnight and signed the Peace of Tolentino on 19 February. Bonaparte then advanced against the Archduke Charles and signed peace preliminaries at Leoben on 18 April. Masséna was later made duc de Rivoli, and Napoleon raised a column on the battlefield that the Austrians pulled down in 1814.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Columns converging across mountains are strong only if they arrive together. A defender who holds the point where they meet can beat them one at a time, if he is willing to leave secondary threats to small forces.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources credit the victory differently: Britannica's biography of Masséna says he won the battle, the Fondation's places page names Bonaparte with Joubert and Masséna, and Britannica's biography of Joubert puts him in charge of the force that held the position. Mantua's surrender is dated 17 January in the Fondation's chronology and 2 February in its article and in Britannica. The column that, in some accounts, tried to envelop the French on the plateau does not appear in the sources read here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon's article from the Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien and Britannica's account of the Italian campaign give the narrative. The Fondation's chronology dates the movements, its places page describes the ground and the monuments, and Britannica's biographies of Masséna and Joubert give their roles.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Directory accepted Bonaparte's proposal in early 1798 to occupy Egypt and strike at Britain's trade and its route to India. The expedition sailed in May, took Malta on 10 June, landed near Alexandria on 1 July and took the city the next day.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Egypt was nominally an Ottoman province but was ruled in practice by the Mamluk beys. In an Arabic proclamation Bonaparte presented himself as a friend of Islam and of the sultan, come to punish the Mamluks. A commission of scholars and scientists went with the army.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Bonaparte aimed to take Cairo and break the Mamluk army under Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey that barred the way.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought before Embabeh, on the west bank of the Nile about 10 km from Cairo and 25 km from the pyramids of Giza, where Murad held an entrenched camp. Ibrahim Bey's force stood on the east bank with a flotilla and took no part.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The French marched in five divisional squares, Desaix's division in the vanguard. Murad's army combined Mamluk cavalry with infantry and guns in the entrenchments. Britannica notes that contemporary estimates of the Egyptian force, Bonaparte's among them, were probably inflated by counting attendants and servants; no figures are given here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The march from Alexandria was hard: Bonaparte's column, harassed by Bedouin and short of food and water, lost men to dehydration and suicide. After beating the Mamluks at Shubra Khit on 13 July, the army reached Umm Dinar, north of Cairo, on 20 July and set out at 2 a.m. on the 21st.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: In mid-afternoon the Mamluk cavalry charged the squares of Desaix and Reynier and was shot down and driven back. While the centre held, the flanks advanced. Rampon's troops, supported by Marmont, stormed the entrenched camp at Embabeh, and many of its defenders were driven into the Nile and drowned. Lasalle's light cavalry completed the rout.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte formed each division into a square, in fact a rectangle six ranks deep with cavalry and baggage inside, that could move and fight in any direction, as he had done at Shubra Khit.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The failure of the Mamluk charges against the squares left the entrenched camp open to assault.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Murad burned his boats and withdrew to Upper Egypt; Ibrahim fled toward Syria with the Ottoman viceroy. French soldiers stripped the Mamluk dead of valuables. In the panic in Cairo many fleeing inhabitants were robbed and killed by Bedouin. The French entered the city within days.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: On 1 August Nelson destroyed the French fleet in Aboukir Bay, leaving the army cut off in Egypt. The Ottoman sultan declared war on France in September, and a revolt in Cairo in October was put down with artillery. Desaix pursued Murad into Upper Egypt.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Disciplined infantry formations could defeat a cavalry army in open battle, but the campaign turned on the sea: within days the loss of the fleet overshadowed the victory.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The name is Bonaparte's choice: the fighting was at Embabeh, and Britannica judges his address about forty centuries looking down from the pyramids likely apocryphal, since they were probably not visible. Accounts differ on when the French entered Cairo (23, 25 or 27 July) and on the time of the Mamluk charge (about 3.30 or 4 p.m.). Thierry Lentz argues that the expedition's glorious image was a myth that took root before Bonaparte had left Egypt.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's battle article and François-Guy Hourtoulle's article for the Fondation Napoléon give the narrative. Britannica's history of Egypt gives the political setting, Thierry Lentz's essay the campaign's later image, and Jacques Juillet's biography of Desaix his division's part.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the loss of his fleet in 1798 Bonaparte was in effect marooned in Egypt, and the Ottoman sultan had declared war on France. Ottoman Syria, dominated by Ahmad al-Jazzar, governor of Acre, was the base from which Egypt could most easily be threatened.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bonaparte invaded Syria in February 1799 to deny it to his enemies.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Bonaparte had to take Acre before Ottoman forces gathering at Damascus could come to Jazzar's aid.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Acre is a walled coastal city in present-day north-west Israel, whose old fortifications and citadel Jazzar had strengthened. Bonaparte camped on Tel Akko, south-east of the city, still known as Napoleon's Hill. Because Acre lay on the sea, it could be supplied while the besiegers could not.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Jazzar's garrison was supported by two Royal Navy ships of the line under Sir Sidney Smith, and the French émigré officer Phélippeaux helped improve the fortifications. The French force included Kléber's and Lannes's troops. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On the march north the French took El Arish and Gaza and stormed Jaffa on 7 March. The town was pillaged, and its prisoners, except the Egyptians among them, were killed; Pauline Lefebvre's account for the Fondation says they were executed to terrify the enemy. Plague broke out in the army, and on 11 March Bonaparte visited the sick in the Jaffa hospital. The army reached Acre on 18 March. The British had already captured a flotilla carrying half of Bonaparte's siege guns.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Assaults on 28 March and 1 April failed for want of heavy guns and ammunition. A relief army was beaten at Mount Tabor on 16 April by Kléber, whom Bonaparte joined with reinforcements. By the end of April enough artillery had arrived to breach the walls, and assaults followed in early May. On 8 May a party got into the town, but its leader was killed and Lannes was badly wounded, and the attackers found successive lines of inner defences behind the breach.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After the first assaults failed Bonaparte turned to formal siege operations, and he sent Kléber against the relief army rather than lift the siege. In May he accepted defeat and ordered the retreat.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Command of the sea decided the siege: British ships took the siege guns, kept Acre supplied and blockaded the coast, so that the French could not evacuate their wounded.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The siege was abandoned in May and the army began a long, hard retreat to Egypt. Britannica calls Acre Bonaparte's first setback of the Egyptian campaign and the end of his hopes of an empire in the East.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Plague and disease killed many soldiers. Desgenettes, the army's chief physician, inoculated himself in April to reassure the troops and banned the word plague. When the siege was lifted he refused Bonaparte's wish to give the sick opium, saying his duty was to preserve life. Plague-stricken soldiers were left behind at Jaffa on the retreat, for which Bonaparte was long criticised.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A land army cannot take a coastal fortress that its enemy supplies from the sea; lost siege guns and disease made the task harder still.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: British propaganda exploited the killing of the Jaffa prisoners, and rumours spread that plague victims left behind had been poisoned with opium. Gros's painting of Bonaparte among the plague-stricken at Jaffa, shown in 1804, was meant partly to counter both; the sources read here do not settle the poisoning question. Dates differ: Britannica gives 18 March to 20 May, its history of Egypt 19 March; Lentz dates the lifting of the siege to 17 May. The number of assaults is given as five in May (Britannica) or eight in all (Lefebvre).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Adrian Gilbert's Britannica article and François-Guy Hourtoulle's article for the Fondation Napoléon give the narrative. Britannica's history of Egypt sets the context. Jean-Marie Milleliri's study of the army's medical service, Guy Ledoux-Lebard's article on Gros's painting, Pauline Lefebvre's account and Thierry Lentz's essay cover Jaffa, the plague and the campaign's reputation.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Back in Egypt after the failure at Acre, the French faced an Ottoman counter-offensive. A Turkish fleet appeared off the coast on 11 July 1799, and from 14 July the Ottoman Army of Rhodes landed in Aboukir Bay.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The French had been cut off since the loss of their fleet in Aboukir Bay in 1798, and the Ottomans, with British support, were trying to retake Egypt. Lentz notes that the French name for the battle, the land battle of Aboukir, was chosen to make people forget the naval disaster.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Bonaparte aimed to destroy the landing before it could expand inland.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Ottomans held the peninsula at the west end of Aboukir Bay. They took the redoubt, whose small garrison under Godard was killed, and Aboukir fort surrendered on 17 July. They made no further advance and entrenched in two lines across the isthmus.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Bonaparte gathered his troops at Ramanieh and reached Alexandria on 21 July. Destaing's and Lanusse's troops attacked on the left, Lannes's on the right and Murat's cavalry in the centre. Dykstra names the Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha; Albanian troops held the first line. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Ottoman first line held two mounds near the shore. Behind it a second line with a redoubt crossed the isthmus, and the pasha's guard surrounded his camp.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 25 July the first line fell quickly. The second held longer: Leturcq was killed and Fugière lost an arm at the redoubt. Murat's charges and a combined attack by Lannes carried it, and the French reached the pasha's camp, where Murat was wounded by a pistol shot from the pasha, who was taken prisoner. The Ottoman soldiers fled into the sea under fire from French gunboats; survivors held out in the fort until 2 August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte attacked both lines in a single day, with infantry on each flank and the cavalry in the centre.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of the redoubt and the pasha's camp, by Murat's cavalry and Lannes's infantry together, broke the second line.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: In Dykstra's words the Army of Rhodes disintegrated within hours, and many soldiers drowned trying to reach their ships. Murat was promoted general of division on the battlefield. By Milleliri's account Larrey's ambulances reached the wounded so quickly that none waited more than a quarter of an hour for a dressing.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Bonaparte left Egypt secretly on the night of 22 August with a few companions, leaving Kléber in command, and in November seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire. The victory disrupted but did not end Ottoman and British efforts to retake Egypt, and the French surrendered in 1801.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A landing is most vulnerable before it consolidates; struck quickly with infantry and cavalry together, it can be destroyed against the sea.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Lentz sees the battle's name as a way to cover the naval disaster, and the victory served Bonaparte's return to France. The sources differ on the Ottoman commander, whom Dykstra names and also links to the army beaten at Mount Tabor while Hourtoulle calls him only the pasha, and on the date of Bonaparte's departure, 22 or 23 August. Losses are not given here because the sources' estimates vary.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: François-Guy Hourtoulle's article for the Fondation Napoléon gives the detailed narrative and Darrell Dykstra's EBSCO entry a summary. Britannica's history of Egypt and Pauline Lefebvre's account give the setting and Bonaparte's departure, Milleliri the medical service, the Fondation's biography Murat's promotion, and Lentz the battle's later meaning.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After seizing power in November 1799, Bonaparte faced the Second Coalition. In Italy Masséna held out against Austrian besiegers in Genoa from 21 April to 4 June 1800, which helped Bonaparte manoeuvre behind the Austrians.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: As First Consul, Bonaparte needed a victory; Britannica says Marengo secured his military and civilian authority in Paris.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Leading the Army of the Reserve across several Alpine passes in May, Bonaparte cut Melas off from communication with Austria and sought to bring him to battle.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought on the Marengo plain, about 5 km south-east of Alessandria, one of the few good cavalry grounds in northern Italy. The Bormida separated the armies. Melas's headquarters was in the citadel of Alessandria, Bonaparte's at the farm of Torre di Garofoli toward Tortona.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Melas's army attacked in columns under himself, Ott and O'Reilly. On the French side Victor and Lannes held the front, with Monnier's division as the only reserve; Desaix had been detached south with Boudet's division, and Kellermann commanded a cavalry brigade. Murat commanded the cavalry of the Army of the Reserve. Britannica's strengths are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Believing Melas was at Turin, Bonaparte had sent detachments to find him. Melas was still at Alessandria, and on the morning of 14 June his army crossed the Bormida onto the plain.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Austrian attack began about 9 a.m. Victor and Lannes disputed the ground but were driven back across the plain, abandoning guns. Around 11 a.m. Bonaparte realised he faced the main Austrian army, recalled his detachments and committed Monnier. By 3 p.m. the French held a ragged line near San Giuliano. Melas, lightly wounded and believing he had won, returned to Alessandria and left Zach to organise the pursuit. Between 4 and 5 p.m. Boudet's division arrived with Desaix. Marmont's guns opened fire, Desaix's infantry attacked the head of Zach's column, and Kellermann's cavalry charged its flank. Zach was captured, the Austrian cavalry was routed, and by nightfall the Austrians were in retreat.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bonaparte's dispersal of his army nearly lost the battle; his recall of the detachments and the combined counterattack of guns, fresh infantry and cavalry won it.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Kellermann's charge into the flank of Zach's column, just as Desaix's attack was losing momentum, turned Austrian surprise into panic.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Desaix was killed early in the counterattack. The next day Melas agreed to an armistice, the Convention of Alessandria, under which the Austrians gave up northern Italy west of the Mincio.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Britannica calls the defeat the beginning of the end of the Second Coalition: Austria made peace at Lunéville within a year, and Britain signed the Treaty of Amiens in March 1802. Desaix was buried at the Great St Bernard hospice, and Murat received a sabre of honour for the battle.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Dispersing an army to find the enemy risks meeting him with only part of it. A reserve that returns in time, and guns, infantry and cavalry used together at the decisive moment, can still reverse a lost battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica shares credit for the victory among Desaix, Kellermann and Marmont. Desaix's words that there was still time to win are reported in the Fondation's biography only as something he is said to have declared. Britannica has Desaix's column turned back by Bonaparte's recall, the biography by the sound of the guns. The battle's glory was promoted afterwards in paintings, monuments and tombs, and the Fondation doubts the tradition linking a plane tree on the field to Bonaparte.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's battle article gives the detailed narrative, and the Fondation Napoléon's places page the ground and its monuments. Jacques Juillet's biography of Desaix, Britannica's biography of Masséna and the Fondation's biography of Murat add the roles of the three generals.

phases.title: Across the Bormida
phases.description: Melas's army crosses the Bormida and attacks about 9 a.m.

phases.title: The French driven back
phases.description: Victor and Lannes give ground; Monnier's division is committed and driven back.

phases.title: Desaix returns
phases.description: Boudet's division arrives with Desaix as Zach forms the pursuit.

phases.title: The counterattack
phases.description: Guns, Desaix's infantry and Kellermann's cavalry break Zach's column.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Bring Melas to battle after cutting him off from Austria.
perspectives.known: He had crossed the Alps into Melas's rear.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where Melas was; he believed him to be at Turin.
perspectives.constraints: Detachments sent away to find the enemy.
perspectives.forces: Victor's and Lannes's troops, Monnier's division and the Consular Guard on the field; Desaix with Boudet's division away to the south.
perspectives.terrain: An open plain favourable to cavalry, with the Bormida in front.
perspectives.logistics: An army that had just crossed the Alpine passes.
perspectives.decision: Once he saw the main Austrian army before him he recalled his detachments, and when Desaix arrived he counterattacked with all arms.
perspectives.outcome: A narrow victory, an armistice and the Austrian withdrawal from northern Italy west of the Mincio.

perspectives.name: Michael von Melas
perspectives.objective: Break out from Alessandria and reopen his communications with Austria.
perspectives.known: The French were approaching the Bormida.
perspectives.uncertainty: The strength of the French army before him.
perspectives.constraints: A slow crossing of the Bormida delayed his attack.
perspectives.forces: Columns under himself, Ott and O'Reilly, superior in guns and cavalry.
perspectives.terrain: The Marengo plain.
perspectives.logistics: Based on the fortress of Alessandria.
perspectives.decision: He attacked, and by mid-afternoon, lightly wounded and believing the battle won, left Zach to direct the pursuit.
perspectives.outcome: Zach's column was broken, and the next day Melas agreed to an armistice.

2 décembre 1805 : La bataille d'Austerlitz
sources.publisher: French Ministry of the Armed Forces

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The 1805 campaign carried the Grande Armée from the Channel camps through the Ulm campaign and into Austria.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Austria and Russia confronted Napoleon within the Third Coalition. The battle took place on 2 December 1805 in present-day Czechia.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon sought a decisive result before the coalition could improve its position. The Allies attempted to turn the French right.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Pratzen Heights dominated the battlefield; Telnitz and Sokolnitz lay in the southern sector.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: French corps under commanders including Soult, Davout and Lannes faced a combined Austro-Russian army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Allied formations occupied the heights before moving substantial forces south against Napoleon's right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The southern fighting developed first. Soult then attacked the weakened center, followed by fighting for the plateau and an Allied retreat.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon committed Soult against the Pratzen Heights as Allied troops moved away.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Control of the center divided the coalition's fight and allowed the French to redirect forces against its southern wing.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French won decisively. Austria signed an armistice on 6 December.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December, reshaping the political settlement after the campaign.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A useful study question is how timing, terrain and concentration interacted. A deliberate risk can only be assessed against the forces available to support it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The popular image of a perfectly controlled trap compresses a contested battle. This overview omits disputed losses and exact minute-by-minute timing.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon timeline and site guide supply sequence and geography. The French Army page represents an institutional commemorative interpretation.

phases.title: Allied movement south
phases.description: Allied forces advance toward Telnitz and Sokolnitz.

phases.title: Assault on Pratzen
phases.description: Soult's corps attacks the weakened Allied center.

phases.title: Contest for the center
phases.description: Counterattacks fail to restore Allied control of the plateau.

phases.title: Allied withdrawal
phases.description: The divided Allied army retreats; French forces press its southern wing.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Win a decisive battle before Prussia joined the coalition and before further Allied reinforcements arrived.
perspectives.known: The Allies had advanced toward him and occupied the Pratzen Heights, which he had left to them. An attack on his right was expected.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether reinforcements marching from the south would arrive in time to hold the southern sector, and when the Allies would weaken their center.
perspectives.constraints: A long line of communication through Austria after the Ulm campaign, and an army that was smaller on the field until its corps concentrated.
perspectives.forces: Corps including those of Soult, Lannes, Bernadotte and Davout, with the Guard and Murat's cavalry.
perspectives.terrain: The Pratzen plateau dominated the center. Streams, ponds and the villages of Telnitz and Sokolnitz shaped the southern fighting.
perspectives.logistics: Far from France, the army needed a quick decision rather than a prolonged campaign in Moravia.
perspectives.decision: He held Soult's corps ready and launched it against the Pratzen Heights once Allied columns had moved south, around 8–8:30 a.m. in the sources. This describes observable decisions, not his private thoughts.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive French victory, followed by an Austrian armistice on 6 December. The image of a perfectly controlled trap compresses a hard-fought battle.

perspectives.name: Allied command: Kutuzov, Weyrother and the allied emperors
perspectives.objective: Turn the French right and cut Napoleon's communications with Vienna.
perspectives.known: French forces appeared weaker on their right, and the Allies held the Pratzen plateau.
perspectives.uncertainty: The true strength and position of the French army, including forces arriving from the south.
perspectives.constraints: A divided command with Alexander I and Francis I present, and a complex plan requiring several columns to march across the plateau.
perspectives.forces: A combined Russian and Austrian army organized in several attack columns.
perspectives.terrain: Moving off the Pratzen plateau to support the southern attack left the center exposed.
perspectives.logistics: Supplies in Moravia were strained. Waiting for reinforcements and for Prussia was an alternative some favored.
perspectives.decision: They committed most columns to the southern attack, weakening the center. Accounts differ on Kutuzov's reservations about the plan; they are not reconstructed here.
perspectives.outcome: Defeat split the army and Austria left the war. Russian and Austrian accounts later blamed each other.

sources.title: Battle of Waterloo
Waterloo 1815
Blücher and the Waterloo campaign
Three plans showing the Battle of Waterloo, 1815 (MPH 1/387)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Napoleon returned from Elba in 1815. A new coalition mobilized against him.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: His advance into Belgium sought to separate Wellington's and Blücher's armies before larger coalition forces arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The French needed a rapid decision; the Allies needed to sustain cooperation despite separate command structures.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Wellington held the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge with forward strongpoints including Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon faced Wellington's multinational army and, later, Blücher's Prussian corps.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Much Allied infantry sheltered behind the crest of the ridge, out of sight and partly protected from artillery. Squares formed against the later cavalry attacks.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Attacks on the strongpoints and center were followed by cavalry assaults, Prussian intervention and the final Guard attack.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Wellington chose to stand with promised Prussian support. Blücher marched toward him after the defeat at Ligny.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Prussian pressure forced Napoleon to divide attention and reserves. The Imperial Guard's repulse preceded general French retreat.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The coalition won on 18 June. Napoleon's attempt to restore his rule failed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign ended with Allied occupation of Paris and Napoleon's final exile.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Coalition cooperation can be an operational capability. Study liaison and marching decisions alongside the actions visible on the battlefield.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: National narratives assign credit differently, including the weight given to the Prussian intervention. The schematic simplifies simultaneous engagements and is not derived from period maps.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Compare the National Army Museum narrative with Royal Armouries and the Prussian-focused Fondation Napoléon dossier. The National Archives holds three 1815 plans of the battle (MPH 1/387); they are catalogued but not digitised.

phases.title: Strongpoints attacked
phases.description: French assaults begin against Wellington's forward positions.

phases.title: Assaults on the ridge
phases.description: Infantry and cavalry fighting tests the Allied line.

phases.title: A second front
phases.description: Prussian forces enter the battle against Napoleon's right.

phases.title: Final repulse
phases.description: The Guard attack fails; the Allied advance and pursuit follow.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Defeat Wellington before the coalition armies could combine effectively.
perspectives.known: Ligny had forced a Prussian retreat, but its direction and recovery remained critical.
perspectives.uncertainty: How much Prussian force could reach the battlefield in time.
perspectives.constraints: Wet ground, elapsed time and competing demands for reserves.
perspectives.decision: He continued the attack while allocating troops to the Prussian threat. The account describes actions, not an invented inner monologue.
perspectives.forces: The Army of the North, strong in artillery and cavalry, with the Imperial Guard as a final reserve. Grouchy's wing had been detached to follow the Prussians.
perspectives.terrain: Rain-soaked ground delayed the attack and hampered artillery and cavalry. Fortified farms broke up assaults before they reached the ridge.
perspectives.logistics: The campaign had to succeed quickly, before larger coalition armies reached France's frontiers.
perspectives.outcome: Defeat ended his return to power. Debate continues over the late start, Grouchy's movements and the use of the cavalry and the Guard.

perspectives.name: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington
perspectives.objective: Hold the position until Prussian assistance could make a combined victory possible.
perspectives.known: Blücher had promised support; his arrival depended on a difficult march.
perspectives.uncertainty: The timing and scale of reinforcement.
perspectives.constraints: A mixed army, an extended defensive line and repeated French pressure.
perspectives.decision: He defended the ridge and strongpoints, then advanced as the French attack failed.
perspectives.forces: A multinational army of British, Dutch-Belgian, Hanoverian, Brunswick and Nassau troops of uneven experience.
perspectives.terrain: The Mont-Saint-Jean ridge sheltered infantry behind its crest. Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte broke up attacks in front of the line.
perspectives.logistics: His communications ran north toward Brussels and the coast. Contact with the Prussians was essential to the plan.
perspectives.outcome: A combined Allied victory. British national narratives long underplayed the Prussian contribution.

perspectives.name: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher
perspectives.objective: Restore cooperation with Wellington after Ligny.
perspectives.known: Wellington intended to fight near Waterloo.
perspectives.uncertainty: March delays and the situation when each corps arrived.
perspectives.constraints: Reorganization after defeat and routes from Wavre.
perspectives.decision: He committed corps toward Waterloo. Their intervention turned a two-army encounter into a coalition victory.
perspectives.forces: Prussian corps regrouping after Ligny. Bülow's corps, which had not fought at Ligny, led the march to Waterloo.
perspectives.terrain: Muddy lanes slowed the march from Wavre. Plancenoit became the focus of the Prussian attack on the French right.
perspectives.logistics: Retreating north to Wavre after Ligny, rather than east toward Prussia, kept the army in reach of Wellington while it regrouped.
perspectives.outcome: The Prussian attack and pursuit turned the French defeat into a rout. Some national narratives have underestimated this role.
